title: On Yap, giant stone money changed hands without moving
body: On the Pacific island of Yap, large carved limestone discs called rai, quarried far away on Palau and up to 3.6 metres across, were used for important ceremonial exchanges. Many were too heavy to move, so ownership passed by public agreement and was remembered in oral history. One stone, said to have sunk during transport, reportedly kept its value because everyone knew who owned it. Economists compare it to modern money, which is mostly a record in a ledger.

slides.question: How wide could the biggest rai stones be?
slides.explanation: The largest discs were up to 3.6 metres across, quarried far away on Palau. Many were too heavy to move, so ownership passed by public agreement.

slides.question: The biggest rai is 3.6 m across. How wide is the smallest, in centimetres?
slides.explanation: Just 3.5 cm across, while the largest, on Rumung island, is 360 cm. Most rai are 30 to 50 cm, and the biggest are too heavy to move.

slides.heading: Fact or myth?

items.text: Rai were quarried far away, mainly on Palau
The biggest rai are about 36 cm across
Ownership could change without the stone moving
Rai were used for everyday shopping

slides.explanation: The discs, up to 3.6 metres across, came mainly from Palau and were used for important ceremonial exchanges, not daily purchases.
